label: Ammonia refrigeration (ice plants, cold stores)
summary: Ice rinks, cold-storage warehouses, meat, dairy and other food and drink plants and breweries often cool with hundreds of kilograms or more of liquid ammonia under pressure. A broken pipe or valve lets out a freezing white cloud that burns eyes, skin and lungs, can roll along the ground, and can explode in a closed room. In 2017 a leak at the Fernie arena in BC killed three workers.
signs: A machinery or compressor room with an NFPA hazard diamond on the door, yellow pipe labels reading 'AMMONIA' in black, ammonia detectors and outside switches for emergency fans
Insulated pipes running to frosty cooling coils in cold rooms; a vent stack, tanks and an evaporative condenser on the roof or outside; a windsock

Ice rinks: in BC, 181 of 223 rinks and recreation sites inspected in 2017 used ammonia. At the Vancouver rink in 2022 the ammonia stayed in the machinery room and the pipes under the ice carried cold brine
A sharp, choking smell: most people notice it at 5 to 50 ppm, find anything above about 100 ppm uncomfortable, and leave at once at 300 to 500 ppm
Your nose tires: with longer exposure the smell fades even though the gas is still there
A white fog near the ground, or frost forming on a valve, pipe or vent line
A shut-down plant still holds its whole charge in its tanks: if that liquid warms, the pressure climbs until a relief valve dumps ammonia out of the vent stack
do: Stay out of machine rooms and plant areas, and leave pipes, valves and coils in cold rooms alone; take what you need from offices, loading docks and other areas where you can't smell ammonia
If you smell ammonia or see the white cloud, leave at once, upwind and uphill, at least 100 m (330 ft) and further downwind of a big leak
Check the windsock and keep out of low ground, basements and pits: the cold cloud from a liquid leak spreads along the ground
Keep away from air intakes near the vent stack: in Vancouver in 2022 a release from the stack dropped to the ground and was drawn into the machine room
dont: Don't cut, unbolt, drill or heat any pipe, valve, vessel or fitting in an ammonia plant, even if it looks empty: much of the system holds liquid ammonia under pressure
Don't open valves, drain oil, or run pumps or compressors on the system: in Vancouver in 2022 a brine pump run against a closed valve warmed the ammonia until a relief valve vented 272 kg (600 lb)

Don't make sparks or flames where ammonia has leaked indoors: at roughly 15 to 28% in air (EPA and CDC say 16 to 25%) it can burn or explode, and oil from the system lowers the limit, to 8% in one study
Don't go in after someone who collapsed in ammonia without air-supplied breathing apparatus
ppe: A full-face mask with ammonia cartridges (green on US cartridges) is for low levels only: NIOSH rates it up to 300 ppm, the level it calls immediately dangerous to life. Above that, or if you don't know, only SCBA works
Splash goggles, with a face shield over them where liquid could spray; never contact lenses
Neoprene or other ammonia-proof gloves, insulated against freezing; cotton clothes rather than wool or synthetics if you have nothing impervious
A dust mask, N95 or other particle mask does nothing against ammonia gas
firstAid: Get them to clean air upwind at once; if they aren't breathing, start CPR

Eyes: flush straight away with plenty of clean water for at least 15 minutes, lids held open, contact lenses out; with no medic to hand, keep going for another 15. Ammonia gets into the eye more than any other alkali, and damage can show up to a week later
Skin: flood it with water at once and take off soaked clothing while you rinse, for at least 5 minutes on liquid burns. Clothes frozen to the skin come off only after thawing them with water
Keep them warm and dry afterwards: water and wet clothes chill people
Anyone who breathed it and coughed or wheezed needs rest and watching: lung injury can keep developing for 18 to 24 hours
